children: The possibility of renewed U.S. strikes on Iran has left the Gulf region tense and weary. According to Sina Finance, Gulf officials are stepping up mediation efforts, concerned that their countries would be among the first affected if the conflict escalates. Several host U.S. military bases and have faced Iranian retaliation.

Qatari mediators arrived in Tehran on Friday to seek ceasefire talks, described by one source as a last-ditch effort to reach an interim U.S.-Iran agreement. The talks continued in Doha on Saturday, with communication with Tehran coordinated with the United States, the source said.

An official familiar with the negotiations said U.S. President Donald Trump was open to an agreement but had not ruled out renewed strikes. Vice President JD Vance, envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner were pushing for a deal, while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and others opposed it, the official said. An Iranian official said the next two days would determine the course of events and added that Washington wanted a positive breakthrough before the U.S. midterm elections.

A White House official said the United States was in a strong position, citing U.S. military progress in the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s difficult economic conditions. The official said Trump would make the decision he considered best for U.S. interests and that Washington remained in regular contact with regional allies.

In Bahrain, home to the U.S. Fifth Fleet for more than 30 years, residents remain anxious after attacks involving hundreds of Iranian drones and missiles. Analysts estimated damage to the fleet’s Manama headquarters and infrastructure at hundreds of millions of dollars. The Strait of Hormuz shipping slowdown and supply-chain disruptions have pushed up supermarket prices.

Gulf governments have called for de-escalation. The UAE Foreign Ministry urged greater diplomatic efforts and a political solution, while Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, called for a Gulf security alliance that includes Iran and Iraq. Gulf states have also expanded defense cooperation with partners such as Turkey and South Korea.

Analysts and officials cited shortages of ballistic-missile interceptors and gaps in regional air defenses. They also voiced concern that a renewed U.S. attack after the midterm elections could put civilian infrastructure at risk. Senator Chris Murphy said a plan to target civilian infrastructure was “crazy” and would inevitably trigger a devastating escalation.

title: Gulf States Push to Ease U.S.-Iran Tensions as Senior U.S. Officials Split
